title: Intoxicants
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley emphasizes the importance of cultivating patience, kindness, and awareness in the face of discomfort, rather than reacting to it with substances or distractions. By practicing being upright through generosity, precept, meditation, and other spiritual practices, we can develop the wisdom to navigate difficult emotions and situations without resorting to escape mechanisms. This approach allows us to find relief from anxiety and discomfort through mindfulness and compassion, rather than relying on external solutions.

sentences.text: Well, good evening, everybody, and welcome, and welcome especially to people who are here for the first time.
It's nice to see new faces, and also nice to see familiar faces.
So my talk today is on the fifth precept, and I'll tell you what that is in just a second.
But in preparing for this talk, like many before me, I read this book, *The Mind of Clover*, by Robert Aitken, and also *Being Upright: Zen Meditation and the Bodhisattva Precepts*, by Reb Anderson.
Reb is a senior dharma teacher and former abbot at the San Francisco Zen Center, who's practiced down there for over 45 years.

And I also went online and listened to a couple of talks on the precepts in general, and I found three different written versions of the fifth precept, which I'll read now, because it'll help us understand the scope of the fifth precept.

So the first wording is the one that probably most of us think of, and it's simply *not giving or taking drugs.* The second version says *not to intoxicate with substances or doctrines, but to promote clarity and awareness.* And then a subparagraph reads, *to share spirits moderately with friends may be all right, but intoxication as a way to relax or cope, whether it be with substances or doctrines, creates confusion or unhappiness.*
And so there's really a big difference between those two.
The first one is very narrow, and I wondered if that might be an old version, mainly for men and women who live in a monastery.

But the second version talks about intoxication, not intoxicating, and actually says that it's okay to drink moderately with friends, and also mentions the possibility of intoxicating with doctrines, with beliefs, with ideas, and then talks about promoting clarity and awareness.
And the third version is Norman Fischer's poetic version, which goes,
*[The reading introduced here is not in the transcript.]*

So when I think about the word intoxicate, I almost always just think about drugs and alcohol, so it was interesting to look the word up in the dictionary and see that it's wider than just drugs and alcohol.
The root of the word toxic is from Latin, which means poison, and to intoxicate means to take in poison.
But a secondary definition means exhilarating.
So one can intoxicate with drugs or alcohol, ideas, beliefs, accomplishments, I think, probably intoxicate with possessions, or with a person, be that a loved one or a leader of some kind.
And that made me think about when our daughter graduated from college.
One of the speakers gave a really good talk.
And this was in June 2002, not very long after the September 11th attacks in New York City.

And the speaker was talking about the problems in the world, and reminded us that a lot of trouble in the world is caused by people who are convinced that they are right and that other people are wrong.
And in the extreme, this is intoxication with doctrines and beliefs, and it's at the root of many of the problems in the world, and also many of the conflicts between individuals.
Just think about it.
How many times have all of us just been convinced, I'm right, and the other person is wrong?
And it just creates all kinds of trouble.
And the most surprising thing I came across in my reading was in Reb's book, in the chapter on the fifth precept.
He grew up in Minnesota, and he left there in his very early 20s to go to San Francisco and began to study Zen, and I believe it was over 20 years before he came back on a visit.
And he tells a story in the book that he went back to Minnesota for a visit in the fall, and it was really cold and clear.
So there was bright sun and blue sky and these beautiful white clouds, and the leaves had turned, so they were just beautiful, and he was really happy and satisfied.
And then one day it rained, and it was gray, and it was still beautiful, but he noticed the thought: it would be better if the sun was shining.
That's a little thing, and we all do that.
I mean, I do that all the time.
Not just about the sun, but all kinds of other things.
And he calls that the impulse to bring something in, to make things different, as opposed to being so much at peace that there's no desire to change anything.
And at first, I was kind of puzzled about putting this in with the fifth precept, because, again, so much I think about it as just about drugs and alcohol.
But it's such a common experience.

And when I read it the first time, some years ago, this story really struck me, because I think it was the first time I started to realize how much I do that myself: if I'm in a line that's moving too slow, or if I'm in traffic, or if it's too hot, or if it's too cold, or the thousands of things we run into each day that aren't just exactly the way we want them to be.

And so I think being dissatisfied with how things are, and wanting them to be different, contributes to the use of food, television, the internet, shopping, all the kinds of things we can do in response to something that's not quite the way we want it to be, as well as drugs and alcohol; to using things like this either destructively or in ways that become addictive.

And so it does seem to me that much of the impulse to use things destructively or addictively is driven by discomfort of some kind, whether it's loneliness or anxiety or boredom or fear or something like that.
And how can our practice help us with things like this, when conditions like this arise?
And here we look at the other parts of the fifth precept, the parts about promoting clarity and awareness, dispelling delusion.
Now, Reb talks about the Buddha Dharma having three aspects.
It has a generosity practice, it has precept practice, and it has meditation practice.
And it's the integration of these three things that he calls being upright, and that's why he titled his book the way he did.

The practice of being upright can happen on the cushion when you're meditating, it can happen at work, it can happen in a relationship, it can happen throughout the day, no matter what conditions you run into.

And we're talking about the ability, the practice being the ability, to open to whatever your situation is, with awareness of the body, awareness of what you're thinking, awareness of what you're feeling, what your emotions are, but also to have patience and curiosity and kindness toward yourself and towards others.
So this is a way to explore a situation without having to change it.
It's like a container for any discomfort, and it helps us avoid reacting to discomfort in a way that increases suffering.

I think Pema Chödrön (some of you are familiar with her; she's a teacher in the Tibetan tradition, who's in her 70s now, and has written a number of books, and is very highly regarded as a teacher), I think she's talking about the same thing in an article on facing difficulties, when she says, and here's a quote from her:
*The Buddhist teachings are fabulous, it's simply the way they are.
They are fabulous at simply working with what is happening as your path of awakening, rather than treating your life experience as some kind of deviation from what is supposed to be happening.
The more difficulties you have, in fact, the greater the opportunity there is to let them transform you.
The difficult things provoke all of your irritations and bring your habitual patterns to the surface, and that becomes the moment of truth.
You have the choice to launch into the lousy habitual patterns you already have, or to stay with the rawness and discomfort of the situation and let it transform you on the spot.*

And staying with the rawness and the discomfort is sitting with it, and being aware of your body, and being aware of your emotions, and being aware of your thoughts, and just with patience and kindness.

So meditation practice is so helpful, not only to assist us in noticing habitual patterns as they emerge and play out, but also to have some ability to just observe, without necessarily speaking or acting or having to change anything.
And that can be a big help in seeing what's underneath our usual responses.
And this is polishing clarity, dispelling delusion, promoting awareness.
Reb talks about: the bodhisattva precepts are not a side issue.
They're at the core of the process of awakening.

And Suzuki Roshi, who's another priest in our tradition, who founded the San Francisco Zen Center, adds another statement: receiving the precepts is a way to help us understand what it means to just sit.
So sitting meditation and precept practice and study just fit so well together.
It's so important to do both.
All of these teachers emphasize the strong connection between meditation practice and precept practice, especially when there's discomfort.
Some of you know this already, but I'm an alcoholic, and I quit drinking a long time ago, before I started meditation practice, actually.
But even though it's been a long time, I still remember very clearly the last year or so of my drinking, and how worried I was about it.
It's a terrible thing to wake up in the morning and have no memory of what happened the night before, and to wonder, what did I say?
What did I do?
What am I going to find out about later?
And once I was able to stay away from alcohol for a few months, I just had this tremendous relief.
I don't have to worry anymore about what did happen or what's going to happen.
Not in the same way, anyway, of course.
But however, once I was away from alcohol for a while, I also realized that alcohol and my social life were just completely combined, and it was really hard to have a social life without drinking.
And I was really anxious and nervous and uncomfortable, and I often didn't know what to say, and didn't feel like I fit in.
And once I started a meditation practice, I still sometimes feel that way.
But along with that then comes just a kind of an acceptance and a patience about that.
So I can feel uncomfortable, but I can also have a little peace about it, and a little patience with it, and it's not nearly as big a deal as it used to be.
So I'm really grateful for that.
And also a meditation practice helps not add a bunch of judgment and criticism, because you can kind of see that and just not feed it.
One of the other great benefits for me has been in my work.

When I get confused, or I don't know what's going on (I do psychotherapy for work, and that happens fairly often, where I'm not sure what to do with someone, or what to say, or how to help), I've become way more patient about that, and just, okay, that's how I feel right now, and we'll just stay with it.
And that's so much better than getting anxious and thinking, oh, geez, I've got to figure this out.
I just feel so grateful for the way meditation practice has helped me at work.
It's really amazing.
So just to be able to notice that, and take a few breaths and relax with it, and not be judgmental about it, is extremely helpful.
And the last thing I want to mention, since I think it applies to the fifth precept, is using prescribed medication for conditions like serious depression or anxiety or chronic pain.
I didn't find anything written about this in my reading.
Although I know things are written about it, I just didn't find any.
So I'm just going to make this my personal opinion.
And I know that prescribed medication can be misused.
I know people can use too much of it, use it too often, use it at the first sign of discomfort, and not do anything else, not try to do anything else to relieve discomfort.
So I know that.
But I do think that if you take the Buddhist concepts of wisdom, compassion and the middle road, prescribed medication can be used in the context of the fifth precept.

And the wisdom part would be working with a physician to discuss your condition, and decide whether or not to take medication, to look at the pros and cons, maybe to try some, and to work with the physician about what dose, how much to take, how often to take.
And if you do that, I think that's using wisdom.

And if you use medication to address significant suffering, but other resources, such as exercise, physical therapy and lifestyle changes, are also included in treating a condition, then I think you're talking about wisdom and compassion.
And then the last thing is the middle road.
The middle road in Buddhism avoids extremes.
So we're talking about avoiding a position where, like, you should never use medication, or you should always use medication.
The middle road allows each person to make a choice about addressing health issues based on what their situation is and what their beliefs are.
And so I think, with those three things, with wisdom, compassion and the middle road, using prescribed medication is not against the fifth precept.
And I think that's everything I wanted to say about the fifth precept.
So thank you very much.
